svg.title: The 32 to 1 collision: why two different groups can share one MAC address and one switch port can receive the wrong channel
svg.desc: Top: the mapping takes 01:00:5e plus the low 23 bits of the IPv4 group address, so 9 bits - the top bit of the second octet plus the entire first octet - are lost. A worked example shows 239.1.1.1 and 239.129.1.1 both mapping to 01:00:5e:01:01:01, because 129 differs from 1 only in the dropped bit. Bottom left: what actually happens on the wire - both groups arrive at a host that asked for one, and only the IP layer of the host filters the extra traffic, so the VLAN and every access port carry both. Bottom middle: the three places the collision bites - the snooping table where one entry serves two groups, the access port where a 4 Mbps stream becomes 8 Mbps, and the ACL audit that cannot tell the two apart. Bottom right: the defence - allocate with the script, check per VLAN, and never rely on MAC-level separation.
svg.text: Nine bits are dropped, so thirty-two groups share one MAC
The switch forwards on MAC. Whatever the IP layer does afterwards, the wire already carried the wrong stream.
low 23 bits of the group address
Dropped: the top bit of the second octet, and the whole first octet (239 or 232 makes no difference to the MAC).
32 groups per MAC, in every combination.
The host asked for one group and receives two.
Its IP stack filters the extra one, so users see
nothing - but the port and the uplink carried double.
One MAC entry serves two groups: a join for one
4 Mbps becomes 8 Mbps on every port with a viewer.
A group-level check cannot tell the two apart:
Compute the MAC for every proposed group
and refuse the allocation on a duplicate.
Two colliding groups in different VLANs are
harmless. In one VLAN they are an outage.
Do not design around the collision, design it
out: one group per MAC within a VLAN.
IPv6 with 33:33 plus 32 bits removes this problem entirely, and replaces it with scope confusion: FF05 forwarded between sites, FF02 used as a service group.
